entries.title: More new US solar is built with batteries attached
entries.summary: Over 16% of the utility-scale solar capacity added in the US in 2026 (through September) is co-located with battery storage, up from 2% in 2017, according to EIA.
points: As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage; the 2017 share was 2%.
Reported plans for the last three months of 2026 could lift the 2026 share to 19%; plans submitted for 2027 and 2028 show more than 30%.
13% of total US utility-scale generating capacity is solar PV, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage.
In California, Arizona, New Mexico and Nevada, the share of solar generation co-located with batteries is more than double the national average.
entries.plain_tip: A plant with both can send its output to the grid or into the battery depending on wholesale prices, which is why developers add storage where solar is large.
entries.caution: Figures are quoted from the publisher and may be revised. For understanding the market only; not investment or trading advice.

entries.title: US wholesale power prices: what EIA expects for 2026
entries.summary: EIA's October 2026 outlook puts the average US wholesale electricity price at $52 per MWh in 2026, 11% above 2025, mostly because of extreme weather.
points: Forecast average: $52/MWh in 2026, 11% more than in 2025, mainly due to winter storm Fern and higher-than-average summer temperatures.
Prices at most hubs have been relatively stable in 2026.
PJM wholesale prices are set to rise 41%, while Northwest Mid-Columbia prices are expected to fall 23%.
EIA finalised model inputs on October 1, 2026; the forecast does not account for later market events.
entries.plain_tip: Treat this as a forecast, not a price quote. The next STEO is scheduled for 2026-11-10 and may change the numbers.
entries.caution: Figures are quoted from the publisher and may be revised. For understanding the market only; not investment or trading advice.

entries.title: Ember: solar met 75% of global demand growth in 2025
entries.summary: Ember's Global Electricity Review 2026 finds clean power met all growth in global electricity demand in 2025, with solar supplying about three quarters of it.
points: Solar met 75% of the net rise in global electricity demand in 2025; its rise was 18 times larger than that of gas, the only fossil fuel that increased.
2025 was the first year since 2020 without an increase in fossil electricity generation.
Fossil generation fell in both China and India as record clean additions outpaced demand growth.
The analysis covers 215 countries, with 2025 data for 91 countries representing 93% of global electricity demand.
entries.plain_tip: Ember uses reported data and says the transition is uneven and incomplete; fossil fuels still play a significant role.

entries.title: Ember: renewables overtook coal in 2025
entries.summary: Ember reports that renewables supplied 33.8% of global electricity in 2025, ahead of coal at 33.0%, the first time this has happened in the modern era.
points: Renewables: 33.8% (10,730 TWh). Coal: 33.0% (10,476 TWh).
Solar and wind growth pushed renewables above a third of global generation.
Ember frames this as the world entering an era of clean growth in the power sector.
entries.plain_tip: Shares are of global generation, not capacity, and rounding follows Ember's overview page.
entries.caution: Figures are quoted from the publisher and may be revised. For understanding the market only; not investment or trading advice.

entries.title: IEA: world renewable capacity could double by 2030
entries.summary: IEA's Renewables 2025 expects global renewable power capacity to roughly double by 2030, adding 4,600 GW, with solar PV making up almost 80% of the increase.
points: Growth of 4,600 GW is roughly the combined power generation capacity of China, the EU and Japan.
Wind capacity is expected to nearly double to over 2,000 GW by 2030; hydropower is 3% of new additions, with pumped storage growing faster than in the previous five years.
The 2025-2030 forecast is 5% lower than last year's, mainly because of policy changes in the United States and China.
Even so, the main case reaches 2.6 times the 2022 level by 2030, short of the COP28 tripling pledge; an accelerated case reaches 2.8 times.
entries.plain_tip: The IEA gives two cases (main and accelerated); say which one you are quoting.

entries.title: IEA: where the forecast changed and why
entries.summary: The IEA cut its US renewables forecast by almost 50% but raised India and Europe, and notes that manufacturers are losing money despite record installations.
points: US forecast revised down by almost 50% after the earlier phase-out of federal tax credits, new import restrictions, a pause on new offshore wind leasing and tighter permitting on federal land.
India is on track to meet its 2030 target, with capacity rising 2.5 times in five years; the EU forecast was revised up slightly on corporate PPA activity.
Corporate PPAs, utility contracts and merchant plants account for 30% of global renewable expansion to 2030, double the share in last year's forecast.
Chinese solar PV prices are down over 60% since 2023; the largest manufacturers' margins are around -10%, with cumulative losses of almost USD 5 billion since the start of 2024.
entries.plain_tip: Policy-driven forecasts move when laws change; check the report date before reusing a number.

entries.title: UK offshore wind auction (AR7): 8.4 GW at about £91/MWh
entries.summary: The UK's seventh Contracts for Difference round awarded 8,437.5 MW of offshore wind. Fixed-bottom projects cleared at £91.20/MWh in 2024 prices.
points: Total awarded: 8,437.5 MW (offshore wind 8,245 MW including 1,380 MW priced separately in Scotland, plus 192.5 MW of floating offshore wind).
Clearing strike prices (2012 prices / 2024 prices): offshore wind £65.45 / £91.20; Scotland £64.23 / £89.49; floating £155.37 / £216.49 per MWh.
Maximum saving against the administrative strike price: 19.29% (offshore wind), 20.81% (Scotland), 20.11% (floating).
By region: England 72.18%, Scotland 17.45%, Wales 10.37% of awarded capacity. First delivery years run from 2028/29 to 2030/31.
entries.plain_tip: Strike prices are quoted in 2012 and 2024 money; compare like with like.
entries.caution: Figures are quoted from the publisher and may be revised. For understanding the market only; not investment or trading advice.

entries.title: UK solar and onshore wind auction (AR7a): 6.2 GW
entries.summary: Round 7a awarded 4,905 MW of solar PV at £65.23/MWh and 1,306 MW of onshore wind at £72.24/MWh (2024 prices), plus 20.9 MW of tidal stream.
points: Solar PV: 4,905.01 MW at £46.82 (2012 prices) / £65.23 (2024 prices); maximum saving 13.03%.
Onshore wind: 1,306.18 MW at £51.85 / £72.24; maximum saving 21.48%. Tidal stream: 20.90 MW at £190.19 / £265.00.
Total 6,232.09 MW: England 68.60%, Scotland 22.88%, Wales 8.52%.
Awarded delivery years run from 2027/28 to 2029/30 (table E).
entries.plain_tip: Compare with AR7 offshore wind (entry en-intl-007): onshore wind and solar cleared well below offshore.
